vectors.name: formats-xml/basic/interleaved-elements-preserve-order
vectors.comment: A map-of-arrays model cannot represent this interleaving; the edge list can. This is the whole reason the Document is an ordered edge list rather than a map -- confirmed against JSON's own parse of the equivalent {"m":[...]} shape, which cannot preserve this order at all.

vectors.name: formats-xml/basic/attributes-are-dropped-on-read
vectors.comment: D-3 (closed 2026-08-23): the attribute x="1" is gone -- there is no path from a Document edge back to an attribute, so writing never produces one either -- and that drop MUST now be reported via format.attribute-dropped (Sec8.3.8), not silent. Path is $.a: the element the attribute was lost from.

vectors.name: formats-xml/basic/namespace-prefix-is-dropped-on-read
vectors.comment: D-3 (closed 2026-08-23): a prefixed tag <ns:b> reads as the local name b, with the prefix and any namespace binding discarded -- reported via format.namespace-dropped (Sec8.3.8), not silent. Path is $.a.b: the element the prefix was lost from, using the same RecordName.label-style dotted path convention Sec8.4 defines for Schema/Document paths generally.

vectors.name: formats-xml/basic/multi-rooted-document-cannot-be-written
vectors.comment: An XML document has exactly one top-level element; a Document with several top-level edges (legal in JSON/YAML/TOML) has no XML spelling at all. This is exactly why the worked examples in every format page wrap the Order under a single top-level `order` key -- XML alone requires it.

vectors.name: formats-xml/basic/label-with-illegal-xml-characters-cannot-be-written
vectors.comment: A space is not legal in an XML name, and there is no single well-defined substitute -- sanitizing it means inventing content, and (confirmed separately) can even make two genuinely different labels collide into the same written tag with no way to detect it happened. The write fails, unconditionally, not just under strict -- this is not a format.* adjustment a caller can opt out of checking for.

vectors.name: formats-xml/basic/empty-internal-node-cannot-be-written
vectors.comment: An empty internal node (zero edges) and an empty-string leaf have no distinct XML spelling -- both would be written as the self-closing <x />, and confirmed live that reading it back always produces the empty-string leaf, never the empty internal node, with no diagnostic distinguishing the two cases that collided. The write fails, unconditionally, not just under strict -- same principle as the label and NaN cases above, not a format.* adjustment that still succeeds.

vectors.name: formats-xml/basic/carriage-return-written-as-numeric-character-reference
vectors.comment: XML mandates line-ending normalization on parse -- a literal \r byte and a literal \n byte, written as-is, are indistinguishable on read-back (confirmed live, this used to be format.string-cr-normalized, a lossy warning-severity adjustment). A numeric character reference is exempt from that normalization, so writing \r as  instead of a raw byte is genuinely lossless, not merely reported-as-lossy -- confirmed live that  survives a compliant parser and reads back as the exact original byte. No diagnostic is needed for this case at all once the writer does this. Per omnist-spec#52: this vector's expect.text is indented, matching the Python reference's own writer default, but that indentation is not itself normative (Sec8.5.3) -- a compact-output writer (e.g. omnist-go's) is equally conformant, and a harness MUST strip insignificant inter-tag whitespace from both sides before comparing, per the new rule in Sec8.5.3. The escaping (, not a raw byte) is what this vector actually tests; the indentation shown here is incidental.
